vs-code.use: When you want a free editor with plenty of extensions that works for almost any language.
vs-code.avoid: If you need deep refactoring for one specific language (a dedicated IDE does more) or you have a very modest machine.

cursor.use: When you want AI built into the editor (chat, multi-file editing) while keeping the VS Code experience.
cursor.avoid: If company policy restricts sending code to AI services, or you don't want to pay for heavy usage.

neovim.use: When you live in the terminal, want speed and are willing to invest time in configuration.
neovim.avoid: If you need immediate productivity without configuring anything, or you work with people who expect a standard graphical editor.

jetbrains-ides.use: For large projects in one main language (Java, Kotlin, Python, JS) where refactoring and analysis make a difference.
jetbrains-ides.avoid: On low-memory machines or if you only edit loose files; most of the IDEs are paid.

zed.use: When you want a very fast editor with real-time collaboration built in.
zed.avoid: If you depend on a large extension ecosystem or use Windows with workflows that aren't supported yet.

sublime-text.use: To open and edit huge files quickly, without waiting for a heavy editor to load.
sublime-text.avoid: If you want AI, debugging and Git out of the box; the plugin ecosystem is smaller than VS Code's.

helix.use: When you like modal editing but prefer LSP and tree-sitter working without configuring plugins.
helix.avoid: If you need a plugin system (still limited) or don't want to learn yet another way of editing.

xcode.use: To develop iOS, macOS and other Apple platform apps; it is the official way to build, debug and publish.
xcode.avoid: For anything outside the Apple ecosystem, or if you don't have a Mac.

git.use: In practically every software project, solo or in a team.
git.avoid: For versioning very large binary files without Git LFS; the learning curve also weighs on beginners.

github.use: When the project is open source or you want the most widespread ecosystem of PRs, Actions and Copilot.
github.avoid: If you need to host everything on your own infrastructure (prefer GitLab or Gitea) or depend on Jira (Bitbucket integrates better).

gitlab.use: When you want repository, CI/CD and project management on a single platform, including self-hosted.
gitlab.avoid: If you only need simple hosting and an active open source community; GitHub has more reach.

bitbucket.use: When the team already uses Jira and other Atlassian products and wants everything integrated.
bitbucket.avoid: For open source projects seeking visibility and outside contributions.

lazygit.use: When you use Git in the terminal and want staging, rebase and branches with a few keystrokes.
lazygit.avoid: If you prefer a full graphical interface or already master the commands and shell scripts.

github-cli.use: To create PRs, view issues and follow Actions without leaving the terminal, or to automate GitHub tasks.
github-cli.avoid: If your repositories aren't on GitHub.

gitea.use: When you want your own Git server that is light and simple to maintain, even on a small server.
gitea.avoid: If you need advanced enterprise features (robust built-in CI, portfolio management) without assembling more pieces.

pre-commit.use: To run lint, formatting and checks automatically before every commit, the same for the whole team.
pre-commit.avoid: If the hooks get slow; leave heavy checks to CI.

react.use: For complex, interactive interfaces, when you want the largest ecosystem and job market.
react.avoid: On simple content sites, where static HTML or Astro ship less JavaScript.

nextjs.use: For React applications that need routing, server rendering, SEO and simple deployment.
nextjs.avoid: If the project is a small SPA with no SEO needs, or you don't want to keep up with the framework's frequent changes.

vite.use: As a dev server and build tool for SPAs and libraries, with near-instant reload.
vite.avoid: If you need ready-made server rendering and file-based routes; then a full framework saves work.

tailwindcss.use: When you want to style quickly, with consistent tokens, without writing and naming CSS by hand.
tailwindcss.avoid: If the team prefers separate semantic CSS, or if HTML full of classes hurts the team's readability.

svelte.use: When you value lean code, a small bundle and a simple syntax for components.
svelte.avoid: If you need the largest ecosystem of ready-made libraries or easy hiring.

astro.use: For content sites (blogs, docs, marketing) where performance and little JavaScript matter.
astro.avoid: For highly interactive applications with a lot of state shared between screens.

shadcn-ui.use: When you want accessible components that live in your code and can be changed freely.
shadcn-ui.avoid: If you prefer a versioned library with npm updates over maintaining copied components.

threejs.use: For 3D in the browser: visualizations, simple games, interactive experiences and 3D products.
threejs.avoid: For ordinary interfaces; 3D costs performance, accessibility and maintenance.

nodejs.use: For backends, command-line tools and scripts in JavaScript or TypeScript, with the npm ecosystem.
nodejs.avoid: For very CPU-intensive workloads, where a compiled language tends to do better.

bun.use: When you want fast install, tests and execution in a single binary, especially in new projects.
bun.avoid: In critical production that depends on native modules or full Node compatibility.

fastapi.use: For Python APIs with type-based validation, automatic docs and good performance.
fastapi.avoid: If you need a framework with admin, ORM and authentication ready to go; Django delivers that.

django.use: For complete web applications in Python, with ORM, admin and authentication already included.
django.avoid: For small microservices or minimal APIs, where it brings more than you use.

express.use: For simple Node APIs and servers, with a huge middleware ecosystem.
express.avoid: If you want end-to-end types, top performance or to run on the edge; there are more modern options.

hono.use: For lightweight APIs that run on Cloudflare Workers, Bun, Deno or Node with the same code.
hono.avoid: If you depend on specific Express middleware or a framework with more conventions.

trpc.use: When front and back are TypeScript in the same repository and you want typed calls without writing a schema.
trpc.avoid: If the API will be consumed by third parties or by clients in other languages.

graphql.use: When several clients need to ask for exactly the data they want, from different sources.
graphql.avoid: In simple APIs; the cost of schema, resolvers and caching usually doesn't pay off.

postgresql.use: As the main database for most applications: relational, reliable and with extensions such as JSON and search.
postgresql.avoid: For minimal-latency caching or highly volatile unstructured data; other options fit better.

supabase.use: When you want a ready-made backend (Postgres, auth, storage, realtime) to get going fast from scratch.
supabase.avoid: If you need full control of the infrastructure or want to avoid depending on a managed service.

sqlite.use: For local apps, prototypes, tests and sites with little concurrent writing, without a separate server.
sqlite.avoid: When many processes write at the same time or the database must be accessed over the network.

redis.use: For caching, queues, sessions and counters where memory speed matters.
redis.avoid: As the main database for data that cannot be lost; persistence is not its strong suit.

mongodb.use: When the data are flexible documents whose shape changes often.
mongodb.avoid: If there are many relations and queries across entities; a relational database is usually safer.

prisma.use: When you want a declarative schema, generated types and a good TypeScript developer experience.
prisma.avoid: If you often need to write complex SQL, or need a very light runtime for the edge.

drizzle-orm.use: When you like SQL and want strong types with little bundle weight.
drizzle-orm.avoid: If you prefer a layer that hides SQL completely.

dbeaver.use: To explore and query several kinds of databases in a single interface.
dbeaver.avoid: If you only use one database and already have its official client, or prefer to work only in the terminal.

docker.use: To package the application with its dependencies and run it the same in development and production.
docker.avoid: In trivial projects, where the container only adds complexity.

kubernetes.use: When there are many services, variable scale and a team that can operate the cluster.
kubernetes.avoid: In small projects or teams without operations experience; a managed platform solves it with less effort.

vercel.use: To publish frontends (especially Next.js) with per-PR previews and little configuration.
vercel.avoid: For long-running backends or when cost at high traffic is a concern.

cloudflare.use: For CDN, DNS, attack protection and edge functions, with a generous free plan.
cloudflare.avoid: If your code depends on Node APIs that the Workers environment doesn't offer.

terraform.use: To describe and version cloud infrastructure as code, across several providers.
terraform.avoid: In projects with few resources that the provider console handles; watch out for state management.

github-actions.use: For CI/CD of projects already on GitHub, with a large collection of ready-made actions.
github-actions.avoid: If the code is on another platform, or for pipelines that need very specific environments.

aws.use: When you need the widest range of cloud services and enterprise features.
aws.avoid: In small projects, where complexity and cost management outweigh the benefit.

grafana.use: To build dashboards and alerts for metrics, logs and traces from several sources.
grafana.avoid: Without a data source already collecting metrics; it only displays, it doesn't collect.

vitest.use: In new Vite or TypeScript projects, with fast tests and a Jest-like API.
vitest.avoid: If the project already uses Jest at scale and migrating brings no clear gain.

jest.use: When the project already uses Jest, or in React Native, where it is the standard.
jest.avoid: In new Vite-based projects, where Vitest is usually simpler and faster.

playwright.use: For end-to-end tests on Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, with auto-waiting and good debugging.
playwright.avoid: To test isolated logic; unit tests are faster and cheaper.

cypress.use: When the team values the interactive debugging interface and the visual cycle of writing tests.
cypress.avoid: If you need several browsers and tabs in parallel at lower cost; Playwright covers that better.

eslint.use: To find errors and enforce code standards in JavaScript and TypeScript, with many rules and plugins.
eslint.avoid: For formatting; leave that to a dedicated tool such as Prettier or Biome.

prettier.use: To end style debates: the code comes out formatted the same way for everyone.
prettier.avoid: If you want to tweak every detail of the style; it is opinionated on purpose.

biome.use: When you want lint and formatting in a single, very fast binary, in new projects.
biome.avoid: If you depend on ESLint plugins that don't have an equivalent yet.

sonarqube.use: When the team wants to track code quality and vulnerabilities over time, in CI.
sonarqube.avoid: In small or solo projects, where a linter already covers what's needed.

claude-code.use: To delegate coding tasks to an agent that reads the project, edits files and runs commands.
claude-code.avoid: Without reviewing the result, or in repositories with sensitive data that must not leave the machine.

github-copilot.use: When you want AI autocomplete and chat inside the editor, integrated with GitHub.
github-copilot.avoid: If you need an agent that acts on the whole project, or the company restricts the use of AI.

postman.use: To test, document and share API collections with the team.
postman.avoid: If you prefer a light local client, or test everything with scripts and curl.

insomnia.use: When you want a lean, open source API client, including for GraphQL.
insomnia.avoid: If the team needs advanced collaboration and documentation, where Postman is more mature.

raycast.use: To speed up your day on the Mac with shortcuts, snippets and extensions in a single launcher.
raycast.avoid: On Windows or Linux, where support is limited.

warp.use: When you want a modern terminal, with command blocks and AI suggestions.
warp.avoid: If you prefer a traditional terminal, with no account or telemetry, or need 100% open software.

figma.use: To design interfaces as a team and hand specs and assets over to development.
figma.avoid: If you work alone and already prototype directly in code.

obsidian.use: To keep local Markdown notes linked to each other, as a personal knowledge base.
obsidian.avoid: For real-time collaboration; it is designed for individual use.

visual-studio.use: To develop in .NET and C++ on Windows with a top-tier debugger and profiler.
visual-studio.avoid: If you work on macOS or Linux, or prefer a lightweight editor.

android-studio.use: To build, debug and publish Android apps, the official path.
android-studio.avoid: For anything outside the Android ecosystem; it uses a lot of memory.

eclipse.use: When your enterprise environment already uses Eclipse or you need specific Java ecosystem plugins.
eclipse.avoid: In new projects where a more modern IDE or VS Code fits better.

netbeans.use: For Java projects with Maven or Gradle when you want a free, easy-to-install IDE.
netbeans.avoid: If you need the broadest plugin ecosystem or deeper code analysis.

emacs.use: When you want a fully programmable environment and accept a long learning curve.
emacs.avoid: If you want immediate productivity without configuration or unusual keybindings.

vim.use: To edit files on servers and in the terminal, on any machine where it is already installed.
vim.avoid: If you prefer modern features out of the box (LSP, async plugins); Neovim goes further there.

nano.use: For quick edits to configuration files in the terminal, without memorizing commands.
nano.avoid: For all-day coding; it lacks features such as multiple cursors and LSP.

kakoune.use: When you like modal editing and prefer composing with Unix tools over relying on plugins.
kakoune.avoid: If you need ready-made LSP and plugins; Helix ships that built in.

micro.use: For anyone who wants an intuitive terminal editor, without learning modes or new shortcuts.
micro.avoid: If you need modal editing or a large plugin ecosystem.

lapce.use: When you want a light, fast graphical editor and accept a still-small ecosystem.
lapce.avoid: If you depend on many extensions or on mature built-in debugging.

vscodium.use: When you want the VS Code experience with a 100% open source binary and no telemetry.
vscodium.avoid: If you need extensions exclusive to Microsoft's marketplace (such as some from Microsoft itself).

notepad-plus-plus.use: For quick, light edits on Windows, from logs to scripts.
notepad-plus-plus.avoid: If you use macOS or Linux, or need built-in LSP and debugging.

doom-emacs.use: When you want the power of Emacs with Vim keybindings, without building the configuration from scratch.
doom-emacs.avoid: If you prefer to understand every line of your own configuration.

lazyvim.use: When you want a productive Neovim from day one, without writing the base configuration.
lazyvim.avoid: If you want to control and understand every plugin in your setup.

alacritty.use: When you want a very fast, minimalist terminal, combined with tmux or Zellij.
alacritty.avoid: If you want tabs, splits and graphical configuration built in.

kitty.use: When you want a fast terminal with splits and images, without needing a multiplexer.
kitty.avoid: If you prefer a minimal terminal or fully graphical configuration.

wezterm.use: When you want a cross-platform terminal with its own multiplexer and Lua configuration.
wezterm.avoid: If you want something minimal, with no configuration file to maintain.

ghostty.use: When you want a fast terminal with a native look and little configuration.
ghostty.avoid: If you use Windows (no official support so far) or need a built-in multiplexer.

tmux.use: To keep terminal sessions alive on remote servers and organize panes and windows.
tmux.avoid: If your terminal already has enough tabs and splits and you don't use SSH.

zellij.use: When you want a friendly multiplexer, with visible shortcuts and ready-made layouts.
zellij.avoid: If you need tmux's compatibility and ubiquity on older servers.

windows-terminal.use: To work with PowerShell and WSL on Windows in a modern terminal.
windows-terminal.avoid: If you use macOS or Linux.

iterm2.use: For macOS users who want a feature-rich, mature terminal.
iterm2.avoid: Outside macOS, or if you prefer a minimalist terminal.

fish.use: When you want a pleasant interactive shell with no configuration.
fish.avoid: For portable scripts; its syntax is not POSIX/bash compatible.

starship.use: When you want an informative prompt that is the same across every shell you use.
starship.avoid: If you prefer a minimal prompt; it adds items that can clutter the line.

oh-my-zsh.use: When you use Zsh and want ready-made plugins and themes to start fast.
oh-my-zsh.avoid: If shell startup time matters; there are lighter alternatives.

nushell.use: When you work a lot with structured data (JSON, CSV) in the terminal.
nushell.avoid: For scripts that must run on any machine; it is not POSIX-compatible.

code-server.use: When you want a browser-accessible dev environment on your own infrastructure.
code-server.avoid: If you need Microsoft's official marketplace support and every extension.

github-codespaces.use: To standardize the team's environment and start contributing without installing anything locally.
github-codespaces.avoid: If you work offline or want to avoid the hourly usage cost.

stackblitz.use: To create JavaScript/TypeScript prototypes and bug reproductions and share them by link.
stackblitz.avoid: For projects that depend on native binaries, databases or other languages.

git-lfs.use: When the repository must version large binaries without ballooning the clone size.
git-lfs.avoid: If the files are small or rarely change; regular history already handles it.

gitkraken.use: When you prefer a graphical interface to see branches and resolve conflicts.
gitkraken.avoid: If you work on private team repositories and don't want to pay; the free plan is limited.

sourcetree.use: For anyone who wants a free graphical Git client, especially in the Atlassian ecosystem.
sourcetree.avoid: On Linux (there is no version) or if you want a lighter, faster interface.

github-desktop.use: For people starting with Git or wanting a minimal GitHub workflow.
github-desktop.avoid: If you need advanced features (interactive rebase, complex multiple remotes).

tig.use: To read a repository's history and blame in the terminal, fast and without leaving it.
tig.avoid: To change the repository state with few commands; lazygit is more complete there.

gitui.use: When you want a light, fast Git TUI, even on large repositories.
gitui.avoid: If you need features such as full interactive rebase, where lazygit is more advanced.

delta.use: To read Git diffs in the terminal with far more readable colors and context.
delta.avoid: If the default diff is enough or you review only in a graphical interface.

difftastic.use: When line diffs get noisy from reformatting and you want to see only the real change.
difftastic.avoid: For languages without a supported grammar, or where plain text diff is enough.

husky.use: In JavaScript/TypeScript projects that want to run lint and tests before committing.
husky.avoid: In projects without Node, or if you prefer a multi-language hook manager.

lefthook.use: When you want fast, parallel hooks in a monorepo or multi-language project.
lefthook.avoid: If the team only uses Node and is already comfortable with Husky.

lint-staged.use: To keep pre-commit fast by checking only what changed.
lint-staged.avoid: If CI already does all the checking and local hooks aren't needed.

commitlint.use: When the team adopts Conventional Commits and wants the format enforced automatically.
commitlint.avoid: In small teams with no commit convention, where the rule just gets in the way.

commitizen.use: To help the team write standardized commits without memorizing the format.
commitizen.avoid: If the team already writes good commits by hand and prefers no extra step.

semantic-release.use: When you want fully automated releases driven by commits.
semantic-release.avoid: If you prefer to review and approve the version and changelog manually before each release.

changesets.use: In monorepos with several published packages, with human control over each version.
changesets.avoid: If you want full automation with no extra files in PRs.

release-please.use: When you want release automation, but with a PR to review before publishing.
release-please.avoid: If you don't use GitHub or Conventional Commits.

git-cliff.use: To generate nice, customized changelogs without coupling to publishing.
git-cliff.avoid: If you need automatic versioning and publishing; it only generates the changelog.

jujutsu.use: When you want to try a simpler version control workflow while keeping the Git repository.
jujutsu.avoid: If the team depends on tools and workflows that assume standard Git.

mercurial.use: When the project already uses Mercurial or you value a more regular command interface.
mercurial.avoid: In new projects: Git has far more tooling and hosting.

forgejo.use: When you want to host your own Git with community governance and easy operation.
forgejo.avoid: If you need GitLab's broad enterprise features.

codeberg.use: For open source projects that want a nonprofit alternative to GitHub.
codeberg.avoid: If you need robust CI, broad integrations or private projects at scale.

azure-devops.use: When the company is already in the Microsoft ecosystem and needs integrated repositories, pipelines and boards.
azure-devops.avoid: For open source projects or teams that prefer the GitHub ecosystem.

gh-dash.use: To follow PRs and issues across several repositories without opening the browser.
gh-dash.avoid: If you don't use the GitHub CLI or prefer the web interface.

renovate.use: When you want highly configurable dependency updates, across several platforms.
renovate.avoid: If GitHub's native Dependabot already works and you prefer less configuration.

dependabot.use: To keep dependencies and security alerts up to date in GitHub repositories with little configuration.
dependabot.avoid: If you need very detailed grouping rules or other platforms.

gitleaks.use: To keep keys and passwords out of the repository, in pre-commit hooks and in CI.
gitleaks.avoid: As your only defense: secrets that already leaked must be revoked, not just removed.

trufflehog.use: When you want to scan for secrets and know which ones still work.
trufflehog.avoid: In environments where testing credentials against external services is not allowed.

sourcehut.use: If you like email-based workflows and fast, light interfaces.
sourcehut.avoid: If you want GitHub's pull request flow and social network.

gerrit.use: When you need a per-change review workflow with approval control.
gerrit.avoid: In small teams or those that prefer the simple pull request flow.

vue.use: When you want an approachable framework with good documentation and a gentle learning curve.
vue.avoid: If your team or local market has already standardized on React.

nuxt.use: For Vue apps that need SSR, SEO and ready-made conventions.
nuxt.avoid: For a small Vue SPA, where Vite alone is enough.

angular.use: In large enterprise applications, with many teams, that value strict conventions.
angular.avoid: In small projects or prototypes, where it brings more structure than needed.

solidjs.use: When you want React-like syntax with fine-grained reactivity performance.
solidjs.avoid: If you need a huge ecosystem of ready-made libraries.

preact.use: When bundle size matters a lot (widgets, light pages) and you want React's API.
preact.avoid: If you depend on recent React features that the compatibility layer doesn't cover yet.

qwik.use: For large sites where initial load time is critical.
qwik.avoid: If the team needs a mature ecosystem and many ready-made libraries.

react-router.use: For React apps that want strong routing and data loading without being tied to Next.js.
react-router.avoid: If you prefer Next.js's ecosystem and conventions.

sveltekit.use: For Svelte apps with routes, SSR and simple deployment on several platforms.
sveltekit.avoid: If you need a larger job market and ecosystem, like React's.

htmx.use: For server-rendered apps that need interactivity without an SPA.
htmx.avoid: For highly interactive interfaces with a lot of client-side state.

alpinejs.use: To add targeted interactivity (menus, modals) to server-rendered pages.
alpinejs.avoid: For large apps, where a full component framework organizes the code better.

lit.use: To build reusable components that must work in any framework.
lit.avoid: For whole apps; it lacks ready-made routing and state like full frameworks.

typescript.use: In practically any medium or large JavaScript project.
typescript.avoid: In tiny scripts or throwaway prototypes, where configuration weighs more than the gain.

webpack.use: In existing projects that already use it or that need very specific configurations.
webpack.avoid: In new projects, where Vite is faster and simpler.

esbuild.use: For very fast builds of libraries, scripts and as a base for other tools.
esbuild.avoid: If you need complex transformations and plugins it doesn't offer.

rollup.use: To bundle libraries with clean output in several formats.
rollup.avoid: For full apps, where Vite already brings a dev server and ready-made configuration.

parcel.use: To get started fast without writing build configuration.
parcel.avoid: If you need the larger plugin ecosystem and community of Vite or webpack.

redux-toolkit.use: In large apps with complex global state and a need for predictability and debugging tools.
redux-toolkit.avoid: In small or medium apps, where simpler state (such as Zustand) is enough.

zustand.use: When you want simple, light global state, without ceremony.
zustand.avoid: If you need strict conventions, extensive middleware and time-travel tools, as in Redux.

tanstack-query.use: In any app that fetches data from APIs and wants automatic caching and refreshing.
tanstack-query.avoid: In apps with almost no API calls, or that already handle this on the server (Server Components).

radix-ui.use: To build your own design system with accessibility solved.
radix-ui.avoid: If you want ready-styled components, ready to use.

mui.use: To build dashboards and internal apps quickly with complete, consistent components.
mui.avoid: If you want your own visual identity outside Material Design.

chakra-ui.use: When you want accessible components styled through props, with a good developer experience.
chakra-ui.avoid: If you prefer utility CSS (Tailwind) or want to avoid runtime CSS-in-JS.

bootstrap.use: To assemble responsive interfaces quickly, without custom design.
bootstrap.avoid: If you want a unique look; sites tend to look generic without customization.

motion.use: For UI animation in React: transitions, gestures and layout changes.
motion.avoid: For simple hover and fade animations, where CSS is enough.

storybook.use: In design systems and component libraries, to document and test UI in isolation.
storybook.avoid: In small projects with few components, where maintaining stories weighs.

react-three-fiber.use: For 3D scenes in React apps, using React components and state.
react-three-fiber.avoid: Outside React, or in scenes that require fine control of the render loop.

d3.use: For complex, unique visualizations that ready-made chart libraries don't offer.
d3.avoid: For common bar and line charts; Chart.js or similar are much faster to use.

chartjs.use: To add common charts to a page with little code.
chartjs.avoid: For custom visualizations or ones with thousands of points; consider D3 or specialized libraries.

react-hook-form.use: For forms in React with good performance and flexible validation.
react-hook-form.avoid: For trivial one- or two-field forms, where local state is enough.

pnpm.use: In monorepos and on machines with many projects, to install fast and save disk.
pnpm.avoid: If the team depends on tools that assume npm's node_modules structure.

deno.use: When you want native TypeScript, permission-based security and built-in tooling (test, lint, format).
deno.avoid: If you depend on packages that assume the Node ecosystem and don't work on the compatibility layer.

flask.use: For small or medium Python APIs and sites, with freedom to choose the libraries.
flask.avoid: For large projects that benefit from ready-made admin, ORM and authentication, as in Django.

nestjs.use: In large backends with several teams that benefit from a rigid, testable structure.
nestjs.avoid: In small APIs or prototypes, where the ceremony weighs more than the gain.

fastify.use: For fast Node APIs, with schema-based input and output validation.
fastify.avoid: If you depend on specific Express middleware or want the lowest possible learning curve.

laravel.use: For complete web applications in PHP, with productivity and clear conventions.
laravel.avoid: If the team doesn't use PHP or needs a minimal API, where it brings more than you use.

rails.use: To build complete web products quickly, with a mature ecosystem.
rails.avoid: For latency-critical services or teams without Ruby experience.

spring-boot.use: In enterprise services in Java or Kotlin that need robustness and a broad ecosystem.
spring-boot.avoid: In small projects or with a team without JVM experience, where lighter options exist.

aspnet-core.use: For C#/.NET backends, especially in companies already using the Microsoft ecosystem.
aspnet-core.avoid: If the team doesn't use .NET and there is no reason to adopt the platform.

gin.use: For REST APIs in Go with a fast router and a lean API.
gin.avoid: If you prefer just Go's standard library, which already covers many cases.

axum.use: For web services in Rust with strong typing and high performance.
axum.avoid: If the team has no Rust experience and the deadline is short.

phoenix.use: For real-time systems with many simultaneous connections, such as chats and live dashboards.
phoenix.avoid: If the team doesn't know Elixir and the project doesn't need high concurrency.

go.use: For network services, CLIs and infrastructure, with binaries that are simple to distribute.
go.avoid: For heavily abstract code or complex domains, where the language's simplicity is limiting.

rust.use: For software that demands performance and safety: systems, WebAssembly and command-line tools.
rust.avoid: For quick prototypes or new teams, where the learning curve slows delivery.

python.use: For automation, data, AI, scripts and backends, valuing readability and ecosystem.
python.avoid: For performance-critical code or native mobile apps.

authjs.use: To add social login and sessions to Next.js and other framework apps, without an external service.
authjs.avoid: If you need ready-made user management, enterprise SSO and administration; consider Keycloak or a managed service.

keycloak.use: When you need SSO, federation and user management under your control.
keycloak.avoid: In simple apps, where operating an identity server weighs too much.

openapi-generator.use: When the API has an OpenAPI contract and several clients in different languages.
openapi-generator.avoid: If the generated code gets heavy or you prefer shared types straight in code (tRPC).

grpc.use: For communication between microservices, with strong contracts and performance.
grpc.avoid: In public APIs consumed directly by browsers, where REST or GraphQL are simpler.

rabbitmq.use: For task queues and asynchronous communication between services with flexible routing.
rabbitmq.avoid: For very high-volume event streaming with replay; Kafka is more suitable.

kafka.use: For high-volume event pipelines, data integration and event-driven architectures.
kafka.avoid: In small systems, where operating Kafka costs more than a simple queue.

bullmq.use: For background tasks in Node apps that already use Redis.
bullmq.avoid: If you don't want to depend on Redis or need long, durable workflows (Temporal).

zod.use: To validate API inputs, forms and environment variables with guaranteed types.
zod.avoid: In very high-performance paths, where the runtime validation cost matters.

pydantic.use: To validate and serialize data in Python with typed models.
pydantic.avoid: In trivial scripts, where plain dictionaries are enough.

socket-io.use: For chats, notifications and live dashboards, with reconnection and rooms ready to use.
socket-io.avoid: When plain WebSocket or Server-Sent Events are enough and you want to avoid its own protocol.

temporal.use: For long, critical processes (payments, onboarding) that must not be lost on failure.
temporal.avoid: For simple background tasks, where a job queue solves it with far less operations.

strapi.use: To give editors a content panel and expose an API to several front ends.
strapi.avoid: For backends with complex business logic, where a code framework gives more control.

pocketbase.use: For prototypes and small apps that need a ready-made backend that is simple to host.
pocketbase.avoid: For large scale or many concurrent writes, where a client-server database is more suitable.

swagger-ui.use: To publish browsable, testable documentation for a REST API described in OpenAPI.
swagger-ui.avoid: If you prefer more editorial, customized documentation with other tools.

apollo-server.use: To build a GraphQL API in Node.js with an established server.
apollo-server.avoid: If the project doesn't use GraphQL or prefers lighter alternatives.

elysia.use: For APIs on Bun with shared types and built-in validation.
elysia.avoid: If you need to run on Node or other runtimes with the same maturity.

mysql.use: When the project or hosting already assumes MySQL, or in traditional web applications.
mysql.avoid: If you need advanced SQL features and extensions, where PostgreSQL usually goes further.

mariadb.use: When you want a MySQL replacement with community governance.
mariadb.avoid: If you depend on recent features exclusive to MySQL or the Oracle ecosystem.

clickhouse.use: For analytics and dashboards over large volumes of events and logs.
clickhouse.avoid: For transactional workloads with many point updates; use a relational database.

duckdb.use: To analyze local files and datasets with SQL, without setting up a server.
duckdb.avoid: For multi-user transactional applications or data that needs concurrent access over the network.

opensearch.use: For advanced text search and log analysis at scale.
opensearch.avoid: For simple on-site search; Meilisearch or Typesense are much easier to operate.

meilisearch.use: To give a site or app instant search, with little operating effort.
meilisearch.avoid: For log analysis and complex aggregations at large scale.

typesense.use: For catalog and e-commerce search with facets and millisecond responses.
typesense.avoid: For datasets larger than the available memory.

neo4j.use: For data where relationships matter: recommendations, social networks, fraud detection.
neo4j.avoid: For simple tabular data, where a relational database solves it with less complexity.

cassandra.use: For large write volumes with high availability across several data centers.
cassandra.avoid: For ad hoc queries, joins and complex transactions.

dynamodb.use: In AWS applications that need predictable latency and scale without server administration.
dynamodb.avoid: For flexible queries and reporting; the access model must be planned up front.

firebase.use: For mobile and web apps that need a ready-made backend, realtime and authentication quickly.
firebase.avoid: If you want to avoid vendor lock-in or need a relational database.

neon.use: For serverless Postgres with per-PR branches and low cost when idle.
neon.avoid: If you need constant minimal latency, with no cold start, or full infrastructure control.

turso.use: For edge apps and one-database-per-tenant models, with SQLite's simplicity.
turso.avoid: For workloads with heavy concurrent writes or that need advanced Postgres SQL features.

minio.use: When you want S3-style storage on your own infrastructure or in local development.
minio.avoid: If you prefer a managed service and don't want to operate storage.

qdrant.use: For semantic search and RAG at scale, with filters and performance.
qdrant.avoid: For a few thousand vectors, where pgvector in your Postgres is already enough.

pgvector.use: When you already use Postgres and want semantic search without adding another database.
pgvector.avoid: For hundreds of millions of vectors with very strict latency requirements.

chroma.use: To prototype RAG and semantic search quickly, locally or on a server.
chroma.avoid: For large-scale production with strict high-availability requirements.

kysely.use: When you want type-safe SQL without the abstraction of a full ORM.
kysely.avoid: If you prefer an ORM with a schema, migrations and a generated client.

typeorm.use: In projects (such as NestJS) that already use decorators and the entity pattern.
typeorm.avoid: In new projects that prioritize strong types and transparent SQL; there are more modern options.

sqlalchemy.use: For database access in Python with fine control, outside Django's ORM.
sqlalchemy.avoid: In Django projects, which already bring their own integrated ORM.

flyway.use: To version the database schema with SQL scripts, in Java or any-language projects.
flyway.avoid: If the project's ORM already generates and manages migrations.

alembic.use: For schema migrations in Python projects with SQLAlchemy.
alembic.avoid: In Django projects, which have their own migration system.

pgadmin.use: To administer and query PostgreSQL databases in a dedicated graphical interface.
pgadmin.avoid: If you work with several kinds of databases; a universal client may be more practical.

tableplus.use: When you want a fast, pleasant database client for everyday use.
tableplus.avoid: If you need a fully free tool with no limit on tabs and connections.

metabase.use: To give the team dashboards and queries over the database, without depending on analysts.
metabase.avoid: For real-time infrastructure metrics monitoring; Grafana is more suitable.

dbt.use: To organize analytical transformations in SQL with software engineering best practices.
dbt.avoid: For projects without a data warehouse, or with few transformations, where simple scripts are enough.

valkey.use: When you want Redis with a permissive license and community governance.
valkey.avoid: If you depend on newer proprietary Redis modules and features.

memcached.use: For simple object and page caching, with minimal resources.
memcached.avoid: If you need data structures, persistence or queues; Redis/Valkey cover that.

couchdb.use: For offline-first apps that sync data between devices and server.
couchdb.avoid: For complex ad hoc queries and large volumes, where better-suited options exist.

netlify.use: For static sites and frontends with simple deploys and per-pull-request previews.
netlify.avoid: For long-running backends or applications that need fine infrastructure control.

railway.use: To put backends and databases online quickly, without configuring infrastructure.
railway.avoid: If you need fixed, predictable pricing or full environment control.

render.use: To host APIs, workers and databases with predictable pricing and minimal configuration.
render.avoid: If you need global edge scale or detailed network control.

fly-io.use: For apps that benefit from running close to users, in multiple regions.
fly-io.avoid: If you prefer a simpler, more abstract platform or don't want to operate containers.

digitalocean.use: For small and medium teams that want simple cloud and predictable pricing.
digitalocean.avoid: If you need the huge service catalog and certifications of an enterprise cloud.

google-cloud.use: For data and AI workloads, or when you already use the Google ecosystem.
google-cloud.avoid: In small projects, where complexity and cost outweigh the benefit.

azure.use: In companies already using Microsoft (Active Directory, .NET, Microsoft 365) that need hybrid cloud.
azure.avoid: In small projects or outside the Microsoft ecosystem, where simpler options exist.

nginx.use: To serve sites, reverse proxy and load balance with performance and control.
nginx.avoid: If you want automatic HTTPS and minimal configuration, where Caddy is simpler.

caddy.use: To publish sites and proxies with automatic HTTPS and little configuration.
caddy.avoid: If you depend on modules and advanced configurations widespread in NGINX.

traefik.use: In container environments, where services come and go and routing must keep up.
traefik.avoid: On simple, static servers, where NGINX or Caddy are more direct.

helm.use: To install ready-made applications on Kubernetes and version the deployment of your own.
helm.avoid: If you prefer plain manifests or declarative tools such as Kustomize.

argo-cd.use: To deploy to Kubernetes with Git as the source of truth, with auditing and rollback.
argo-cd.avoid: If you don't use Kubernetes or the team is too small to operate GitOps.

ansible.use: To configure servers and automate repetitive operations tasks, over SSH.
ansible.avoid: To provision cloud infrastructure from scratch; Terraform is more suitable.

pulumi.use: When the team prefers to describe infrastructure in a real programming language.
pulumi.avoid: If the team already masters Terraform and its module ecosystem serves well.

opentofu.use: When you want the Terraform workflow with an open source license and community governance.
opentofu.avoid: If you depend on features exclusive to HashiCorp's latest Terraform version.

prometheus.use: To monitor services and infrastructure, especially on Kubernetes.
prometheus.avoid: To store logs or traces, or metrics for a long time without an additional storage layer.

loki.use: To centralize application and container logs at low cost, alongside Grafana.
loki.avoid: For advanced full-text search in logs; a search engine is more suitable.

opentelemetry.use: To instrument apps once and choose or switch the observability backend later.
opentelemetry.avoid: In small projects, where a single vendor's agent is enough.

datadog.use: When you want complete observability without operating the monitoring infrastructure.
datadog.avoid: If the budget is tight; cost grows fast with data volume.

podman.use: When you want more secure (rootless) containers or to avoid the daemon and Docker Desktop licensing.
podman.avoid: If the team and tools depend on specific Docker integrations.

docker-compose.use: For development environments and simple deployments with several containers.
docker-compose.avoid: For production at scale and high availability, where an orchestrator such as Kubernetes is suited.

k3s.use: To run Kubernetes on small servers, Raspberry Pi and labs.
k3s.avoid: In large production clusters that require a managed environment and full support.

vault.use: To centralize secrets and issue temporary credentials in larger infrastructures.
vault.avoid: In small projects, where the provider's environment variables are enough and operating Vault weighs. BUSL license since 2023.

jenkins.use: When you need self-hosted, highly customizable CI/CD, or already have pipelines on it.
jenkins.avoid: In new projects with no self-hosting requirement, where a managed CI takes less work.

circleci.use: For pipelines that need parallelism, caching and specialized runners.
circleci.avoid: If the code is already on GitHub and GitHub Actions is enough; one less tool to pay for.

turborepo.use: In JS/TS monorepos, to speed up build, test and lint with caching.
turborepo.avoid: In single-package repositories, where caching and the task graph make no difference.

nx.use: In large monorepos that want to run only what was affected and standardize project generation.
nx.avoid: In small monorepos, where a lighter tool (such as Turborepo) is enough.

k9s.use: To operate Kubernetes clusters day to day, with fewer kubectl commands.
k9s.avoid: If you prefer pure command line (kubectl) or a full web interface.

coolify.use: To have a PaaS experience on your own servers, with a low fixed cost.
coolify.avoid: If you don't want to administer servers, updates and backups.

tailscale.use: To access servers and development machines securely, without setting up a VPN.
tailscale.avoid: If policy requires all network infrastructure to be your own, with no third-party coordination service.

testing-library.use: To test UI components (React, Vue, etc.) by the behavior visible to users.
testing-library.avoid: To test pure logic with no interface, where a simple unit test is enough.

mocha.use: In existing Node projects that use Mocha, or when you want to assemble your own tool combination.
mocha.avoid: In new projects that prefer a complete built-in solution (Vitest, Jest).

selenium.use: In existing suites or when the team tests in Java/C# with a browser grid.
selenium.avoid: In new projects, where Playwright is usually faster and more stable.

puppeteer.use: To generate PDFs and screenshots and automate tasks in Chrome via Node.
puppeteer.avoid: For complete E2E test suites across several browsers; Playwright is more complete.

k6.use: To test the load and performance of APIs, with scripts versioned in the repository.
k6.avoid: For browser interface tests; use an E2E tool.

pytest.use: To test any Python project, from scripts to large applications.
pytest.avoid: Rarely; only if the project requires the standard library's unittest by constraint.

junit.use: To test any Java or Kotlin project.

msw.use: To test and develop the front end without depending on a running backend.
msw.avoid: If you prefer integration tests against the real backend.

faker.use: To create realistic test data and seeds without using real data.
faker.avoid: When tests need deterministic, fixed data that you control by hand.

stylelint.use: To keep CSS consistent and free of common errors, in the editor and in CI.
stylelint.avoid: In projects that use only utilities (Tailwind) and have almost no custom CSS.

oxlint.use: For very fast linting in large projects, alone or alongside ESLint.
oxlint.avoid: If you depend on ESLint plugins with no equivalent.

ruff.use: For linting and formatting Python projects in one fast tool.
ruff.avoid: If you depend on Pylint plugins or checks it doesn't implement yet.

mypy.use: To add type safety to Python projects in CI.
mypy.avoid: In small scripts with no type annotations, where the gain is low.

pyright.use: For fast type checking in Python, in the editor and in CI.
pyright.avoid: If the project already has a mature mypy setup and its own plugins.

golangci-lint.use: To standardize Go code quality in the editor and in CI.
golangci-lint.avoid: In tiny projects, where go vet and gofmt are enough.

shellcheck.use: To review shell scripts in the editor and in CI before they break in production.

hadolint.use: To keep Dockerfiles lean and safe, in CI and in the editor.
hadolint.avoid: If the project doesn't use Docker.

semgrep.use: To find vulnerabilities and enforce custom code patterns in CI.
semgrep.avoid: As your only security control; static analysis doesn't replace review and tests.

snyk.use: To monitor dependency and container vulnerabilities with fix suggestions.
snyk.avoid: If the budget is limited and the free tools (Dependabot, Trivy) are enough.

trivy.use: To scan Docker images and dependencies in CI at no cost.
trivy.avoid: If you need centralized vulnerability management and context-based prioritization.

codecov.use: To track test coverage and block PRs that reduce it.
codecov.avoid: If coverage isn't a relevant metric for the team; high numbers don't guarantee good tests.

knip.use: To clean up dependencies and dead code in projects that grew unchecked.
knip.avoid: In small projects, or with a lot of dynamically loaded code it can't trace.

lighthouse.use: To audit pages and track Core Web Vitals in CI and in the browser.
lighthouse.avoid: As a single measure: lab results vary and don't replace real-user data.

axe-core.use: To detect accessibility problems automatically in tests and in CI.
axe-core.avoid: As the only check: automated tools catch only part of the problems; manual testing is still needed.

locust.use: When the team uses Python and wants flexible load scenarios in code.
locust.avoid: For very high load per machine, where tools in Go or Rust yield more.

testcontainers.use: For integration tests against real databases and services, without mocks.
testcontainers.avoid: In CI environments without Docker, or in tests that must be extremely fast.

stryker.use: To evaluate the real quality of the test suite for critical parts of the code.
stryker.avoid: In slow suites or large projects without filtering; execution takes long.

dprint.use: To format large projects with speed and style control.
dprint.avoid: If Prettier is already the standard in the ecosystem and the team.

chromatic.use: To detect visual regressions in design systems and component libraries.
chromatic.avoid: In projects without Storybook or with few visual components.

aider.use: When you want an open source terminal coding agent that works with several models.
aider.avoid: If you prefer a graphical interface in the editor or don't want to send code to AI services.

cline.use: To have an autonomous agent in VS Code with the API key and model of your choice.
cline.avoid: If you don't want to pay for API usage or prefer simple autocomplete.

continue.use: To have a configurable AI assistant in the editor, including with local models.
continue.avoid: If you want a ready-made experience, without configuring models and providers.

codex-cli.use: To delegate coding tasks to a terminal agent using OpenAI models.
codex-cli.avoid: If you prefer another model provider or can't send code to external services.

gemini-cli.use: For a terminal agent with Gemini models and a generous free tier.
gemini-cli.avoid: If you prefer another provider or can't send code to external services.

ollama.use: To use open LLMs locally, with privacy, offline and at no per-use cost.
ollama.avoid: If your hardware is weak or you need the quality of the largest frontier models.

lm-studio.use: To try local models with a graphical interface, without using the terminal.
lm-studio.avoid: If you need open source or command-line automation (Ollama).

llama-cpp.use: For fine control and maximum performance when running local models on varied hardware.
llama-cpp.avoid: If you want something simple to install and use; Ollama and LM Studio package it better.

vercel-ai-sdk.use: To integrate LLMs into TypeScript/React apps with streaming, tools and easy provider switching.
vercel-ai-sdk.avoid: If the project is in Python or needs complex orchestration of long-running agents.

langchain.use: To prototype LLM applications that combine models, tools and data sources.
langchain.avoid: In simple cases, where calling the model API directly is clearer and lighter.

llamaindex.use: To build question-answering systems over your own documents and data (RAG).
llamaindex.avoid: If the application doesn't depend on your own data; a simple model SDK is enough.

hugging-face.use: To find, download and share open models and datasets, and run them in Python.
hugging-face.avoid: If you only need to call a hosted model API from a commercial provider.

mcp.use: To give AI assistants and agents standardized access to tools and data sources.
mcp.avoid: If the integration is a single, simple one, where a direct API call solves it.

n8n.use: To automate processes between services with visual flows and custom logic.
n8n.avoid: If you require a pure open source license (the license is fair-code) or very complex flows that call for code.

v0.use: To quickly create interface prototypes and component starting points.
v0.avoid: To ship final code without review; the output needs tweaks and accessibility work.

chatgpt.use: To answer questions, generate and review code and analyze documents day to day.
chatgpt.avoid: For sensitive data without the proper contractual guarantees, or as the sole source of truth.

claude.use: To code, review code and work with long documents and contexts.
claude.avoid: For sensitive data without the proper contractual guarantees, or as the sole source of truth.

notion.use: For collaborative team documentation and project management.
notion.avoid: If you prioritize local Markdown files, offline use and full data ownership.

linear.use: For software teams that want to track issues, cycles and roadmap without friction.
linear.avoid: If you need highly customized workflows and complex enterprise reporting, as in Jira.

excalidraw.use: To sketch architectures and ideas quickly, alone or collaboratively.
excalidraw.avoid: For formal, standardized diagrams in versioned documentation; prefer text (Mermaid).

mermaid.use: To keep diagrams versioned alongside code and documentation.
mermaid.avoid: For very large diagrams or ones with fine visual layout control.

bitwarden.use: To manage personal and team passwords with open, auditable code.
bitwarden.avoid: If you prefer the operating system's native keychain ecosystem.

homebrew.use: To install and update development tools on macOS and Linux.
homebrew.avoid: On Windows, where native managers such as winget exist.

fzf.use: To find files, history commands and branches quickly in the terminal.
fzf.avoid: If you barely use the terminal.

ripgrep.use: To search for text in large codebases in the terminal.
ripgrep.avoid: If you need POSIX grep-specific features in highly portable scripts.

jq.use: To inspect and transform API responses and JSON files in the terminal and in scripts.
jq.avoid: For complex transformations, where a Python or JavaScript script is more readable.

bat.use: To read files in the terminal with colors and context.
bat.avoid: In scripts, where traditional cat is more predictable and portable.

httpie.use: To test APIs quickly in the terminal with a more readable syntax than curl's.
httpie.avoid: If you need shared collections and documentation, where a graphical client is better.

bruno.use: When you want to version API collections in Git alongside the code, without depending on a cloud.
bruno.avoid: If the team needs real-time collaboration and cloud workspaces.

neovide.use: When you use Neovim and want its own window, with animations and ligature fonts, without leaving your workflow.
neovide.avoid: If you prefer to run Neovim inside the terminal or need the lowest resource use.
